results.title: Weight stability intervals for multi-criteria decision analysis using the weighted sum model - ScienceDirect
results.content: ## Expert Systems with Applications. Volume 296, Part B, 15 January 2026, 128460. # Weight stability intervals for multi-criteria decision analysis using the weighted sum model. Author links open overlay panel, , , ,. Under a Creative Commons license. ## Abstract. Multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA), or multi-criteria decision making (MCDM) encompasses a wide set of mathematical methods to compare alternatives whilst considering multiple criteria and the relative importance (weight) of each criterion or the allowable trade-off between criteria. MCDA/MCDM may be implemented in a decision support system to aid decision makers compare multiple alternatives. A key consideration in any MCDA is the sensitivity of the results obtained to alterations of the criteria weights used. Prior methods to determine the weight stability interval (, the range of values for individual weights for which the ranking of alternatives will not change) include the manual alteration of criteria weights, the use of different sets of criteria weights in a form of scenario analysis, or the process of iteratively searching for the maximum and minimum allowable alterations to individual criteria weights to determine the weight stability interval. The first contribution of this paper is the development of a novel method for determining precise weight stability intervals which does not rely on enumeration or simulation for use with the weighted sum model (WSM, based on the Minkowski norm), one of the most widely used aggregation methods within MCDA. The second contribution of this work is the use of these s to identify the most sensitive weight(s) based on a Pareto dominance approach whilst considering both the allowable increase and decrease in criteria weights. The above points are demonstrated and applied in an analysis of several alternatives for renewable energy (biogas) production. ## Keywords. Multi-criteria decision making sensitivity analysis. ## Data availability. Data will be made available on request. ## Cited by (0).

results.title: Multi-Criteria Decision-Making for the National Park Service’s Deferred Maintenance Budget Allocation | by Patrick Fitzgibbon | Medium
results.content: # Multi-Criteria Decision-Making for the National Park Service’s Deferred Maintenance Budget Allocation. The NPS manages 400+ parks, but only 60 main parks so to make the project more manageable we scoped it down to just allocating funds between the 60 main parks’ critical and non-critical needs (120 different fund needs). Then we just needed an algorithm to allocate the funds to the 120 different needs, based off those metrics, including stakeholder preferences…. For calculating stakeholder preference weights we chose the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP), used Technique for Order of Preference by Similarity to Ideal Solution (TOPSIS) to score parks based on the metrics, then designed a Goal Programming linear program to perform the allocation. NPS budget allocation needed a weight elicitation method to assign stakeholder preferences to the different criteria used to differentiate the parks, then a scoring mechanism to turn the preferences and metrics into holistic scores. A professor gave us a hint to look into the sub-field of Operations Research (OR) called Multi-Criteria Decision-Making (MCDM), which was not actually a subject covered in our undergrad coursework. MADM deals with eliciting numerical weights to represent stakeholder preferences for factors in a decision and the equations needed to turn weights and metrics into scores. The scoring mechanism of AHP is Weighted Sum Method (WSM), but we chose to use the MADM method called TOPSIS instead. This makes WSM more susceptible to rank reversal when stakeholder preferences change — meaning more volatility in scoring than TOPSIS when slight changes in weights or metric values are enacted. What I developed we coined a “Normalized Weighted Sum Multi-Objective Integer Linear Program”, but in retrospect it was Goal Programing (GP). This also made the objectives competing, allocate based off a score versus allocate equally, stakeholder weights were also set for these objectives using AHP. We ran the weights through the program with differing funding amounts to assess the resulting allocation, and as a last minute request— added a Pareto Frontier analysis. We used Excel Solver and VBA to create a program to pull the stakeholder weights from one sheet, the funding amount from another, then loop through the sub-objectives then the main objective of the linear program [which was on yet another sheet].
